blocks.md: **Lists have no indices — so we invent coordinates using RELATIVE pointer motion.**

items.q: All three families share what primitive?

blocks.label: detect (LC141) + find start (LC142)
blocks.py:
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
    if slow == fast:                 # CYCLE confirmed
        slow = head                  # reset one to head
        while slow != fast:          # walk BOTH 1-step
            slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next
        return slow                  # cycle ENTRY node

blocks.md: **Why start-finder works (say it verbatim):** meeting point is k steps into ring where k = distance from head-to-entry; walking both at speed 1 re-synchronizes exactly at entry. Proof lives in modular arithmetic — offer it if pushed.

dummy = Node(0); tail = dummy
while l1 and l2:

    else:                tail.next, l2 = l2, l2.next
    tail = tail.next
tail.next = l1 or l2                 # drain leftover
return dummy.next

blocks.md: **Dummy-head pattern deletes ALL special cases — tail always exists, return dummy->next. Use it in every construction problem from now on.**

items.title: Middle of Linked List

solutionCode.label: fast/slow race — fast moves twice per slow step
solutionCode.py:
def middle_node(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:      # this condition picks the SECOND middle
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    return slow

items.complexity: Time O(n) in a single pass, space O(1).

followups.q: How would you get the FIRST middle instead?
followups.a: Change the loop to `while fast.next and fast.next.next`. The condition decides the bias: stopping when fast can no longer take a full double step leaves slow on the second middle; stopping one step earlier leaves it on the first. Know which one the problem wants before writing the condition.

followups.q: Why does fast move exactly twice as fast?
followups.a: When fast has covered 2k nodes, slow has covered k. Fast reaches the end at n, so slow is at n/2 — the midpoint falls out of the ratio with no length pass. Any ratio works for splitting the list at a fraction; 2:1 gives the middle.

solutionCode.label: Floyd: a faster runner laps a slower one on a circular track

followups.q: Why must they meet rather than skip past each other?
followups.a: Once both are inside the cycle, the gap between them closes by exactly one node per step, because fast gains one net position each iteration. A gap that decreases by one can never jump over zero — it must land on it. That is why a 2:1 ratio is guaranteed to meet and a 3:1 ratio is not.

followups.q: Why compare identity rather than value?
followups.a: Two different nodes can hold the same value, so comparing slow.val == fast.val reports a cycle on any list with duplicates. The question is whether they are the same node — `is` in Python, pointer equality in C++.

items.title: Linked List Cycle II — entry node
items.statement: Return cycle entry; explain the k-step proof.

solutionCode.label: detect, then reset one runner to the head and march in step
solutionCode.py:
def detect_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:                 # phase 1: find ANY meeting point
            p = head                     # phase 2: reset one to the head
            while p is not slow:         # 1 step each
                p = p.next
                slow = slow.next
            return p                     # they meet AT the cycle entry
    return None

followups.q: Give the k-step proof.
followups.a: Let the entry be L nodes from the head and the meeting point be m nodes into a cycle of length C. Slow travelled L + m; fast travelled twice that, and also L + m + kC for some k laps. So 2(L+m) = L + m + kC, giving L + m = kC, hence L = kC − m. Walking L steps from the head and L steps from the meeting point both land on the entry, because kC − m steps forward from m is exactly the entry after k laps.

followups.q: Why does the second phase move both pointers at the same speed?
followups.a: The proof shows the head is L steps from the entry and the meeting point is also L steps from it (mod C). Equal distances mean equal speeds — using 2:1 again would overshoot. The speed change between the two phases is the part people forget.

items.title: Palindrome Linked List
items.statement: O(n)/O(1): mid → reverse second half → compare → (restore bonus).

solutionCode.label: find mid, reverse the tail, compare, then restore
solutionCode.py:
def reverse_from(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        ahead = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = ahead
    return prev


def is_palindrome_list(head) -> bool:
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return True
    slow = fast = head
    while fast.next and fast.next.next:    # FIRST middle: tail starts after slow
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    second = reverse_from(slow.next)

    ok = True
    a, b = head, second
    while b:
        if a.val != b.val:
            ok = False
            break
        a, b = a.next, b.next

    slow.next = reverse_from(second)       # RESTORE: leave the caller's list intact
    return ok

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) — the reversal is in place. Restoring afterwards keeps the input unmutated.

followups.q: Why compare only until the second half runs out?
followups.a: On an odd-length list the middle node belongs to neither half and never needs checking — a palindrome is symmetric around it. Driving the loop off the shorter (second) half handles both parities with one condition, instead of computing how many comparisons to make.

followups.q: Why bother restoring the list?
followups.a: A predicate named "is..." should not mutate its argument. Leaving the second half reversed means a caller who checks twice gets different answers, and any concurrent reader sees a corrupted list. Restoring costs one more O(n) pass and is the difference between a trick and a function you would ship.

items.title: Remove Nth Node From End

solutionCode.label: open a gap of n, then walk both until the leader falls off

items.complexity: Time O(n) in ONE pass, space O(1).

followups.q: Why start both pointers at the dummy rather than the head?
followups.a: Starting at the dummy means back lands on the node BEFORE the target, which is exactly what you need to unlink it. Starting at the head leaves back on the target itself, with no way back to its predecessor — and removing the head then needs its own branch.

followups.q: Why does the loop test front.next rather than front?
followups.a: You want front to stop on the last node, not one past it, so that back stops one before the target. Testing front alone advances one step too far and deletes the wrong node — an off-by-one that only shows up when n equals the list length.

items.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
items.statement: Section code verbatim; then recursive variant aloud.

solutionCode.label: dummy + tail, then drain whatever remains

items.complexity: Time O(m + n), space O(1) iteratively — O(m + n) stack for the recursive form.

followups.q: Why is the drain line a single assignment rather than two loops?
followups.a: The while loop only exits when at least one list is exhausted, so at most one still has nodes — and it is already sorted and already linked. Appending its head splices the entire remainder in O(1). Writing two drain loops works but does O(n) pointer writes for no benefit.

followups.q: Which form would you ship?
followups.a: The iterative one. It is O(1) space where the recursion is O(m+n) stack, and at 10^4 nodes the recursive version risks a stack overflow. The recursive form is worth knowing because it is the natural shape for merge sort on lists, where the depth is only log n.

items.title: Intersection of Two Lists
items.statement: O(1) memory: pointers swap heads at ends — equalize distances.
hints: a reaches end→jump b-head; vice versa.
They meet at intersection or both hit null together.

solutionCode.label: swap heads at the end so both walk m + n total

followups.q: Why does the swap equalise the distances?
followups.a: Let the lists have unique prefixes of length m and n and a shared tail of length c. Pointer p walks m + c + n before reaching the intersection on its second pass; q walks n + c + m. Those are equal, so they arrive simultaneously. The swap manufactures equal path lengths without ever measuring either list.

followups.q: Why does this terminate when there is no intersection?
followups.a: Both pointers walk m + n + 1 steps and become null at the same moment, so p is q (both None) and the loop exits returning null. Without the switch, one would hit null first and the comparison would never match — the symmetry is what guarantees termination in both cases.

items.title: Delete Node Given Only It
hints: Copy next.val into cur; bypass next.

solutionCode.label: you cannot delete this node, so become the next one
solutionCode.py:
def delete_node(node) -> None:
    """Given ONLY the node to delete -- no head, no predecessor."""
    node.val = node.next.val      # impersonate the successor
    node.next = node.next.next    # then unlink the successor instead

followups.q: Why is the tail case impossible?
followups.a: Deleting a node means making its predecessor skip it, and you have no way to reach the predecessor. The trick works by deleting the SUCCESSOR while stealing its value — a tail has no successor, so there is nothing to steal and nothing to unlink. That is why the problem guarantees the node is not last.

followups.q: What does an external pointer to the successor observe?
followups.a: Its node has been freed, so it is dangling — in C++ that is a use-after-free waiting to happen. The list looks correct from the head, but any other reference to the successor is now invalid. Worth naming: this trick trades pointer safety for O(1) deletion.

items.title: Odd Even Linked List
items.statement: Index-odd chain then even chain, stitched.

solutionCode.label: two chains built in parallel, stitched at the end
solutionCode.py:
def odd_even_list(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head
    odd, even = head, head.next
    even_head = even
    while even and even.next:
        odd.next = even.next        # odd takes the node after even
        odd = odd.next
        even.next = odd.next        # even takes the node after that
        even = even.next
    odd.next = even_head            # stitch the even chain onto the odd tail
    return head

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) — nodes are relinked, not copied.

followups.q: Why save evenHead before the loop?
followups.a: The loop advances even until it falls off the end, so the reference to the start of the even chain is lost. Saving it first is the only way to stitch it on afterwards. Forgetting it returns a correct odd chain terminating in null and silently drops half the list.

followups.q: Why is the loop condition on even and not odd?
followups.a: even always trails odd by one node, so even runs out first. Testing even and even.next guarantees both pointer dereferences inside the body are safe. Testing odd would let even become null and crash on even.next.

items.title: Delete Middle Node
items.statement: Track prev of slow while racing.
hints: prev trails slow by lagging assignment.

solutionCode.label: race to the middle while a third pointer trails slow
solutionCode.py:
def delete_middle(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return None                  # 1 node -> empty list
    slow = fast = head
    prev = None
    while fast and fast.next:
        prev = slow                  # trail by assigning BEFORE slow advances
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    prev.next = slow.next
    return head

items.complexity: Time O(n) in one pass, space O(1).

followups.q: Why must prev be assigned before slow moves?
followups.a: prev has to end up one node behind slow. Assigning prev = slow at the top of the body captures slow's position before it advances, so after the step prev trails by exactly one. Assigning after the advance makes prev equal slow and the unlink becomes a self-loop.

followups.q: Why does a single-node list return null?
followups.a: Its only node is the middle, so deleting it empties the list. The loop never runs (fast.next is null), leaving prev as null and prev.next a crash. Handling the one-node case up front is cheaper than guarding inside the loop.
